The truce, which was initially agreed upon by the warring parties in an effort to reduce civilian casualties and create space for negotiations, lapsed without a renewal or a new framework being put forward.

Since the ceasefire’s expiration, officials and observers have reported an absence of any substantive talks or coordinated de‑escalation measures, leaving the situation unchanged and the risk of renewed fighting heightened. The lack of an agreed‑upon off‑ramp underscores the ongoing stalemate and suggests that both sides remain entrenched, with no immediate indication of progress toward a lasting settlement.
author: BBC World

title: Kim Jong Un’s sister ‘unaware’ of talks between US, North Korea
content:
North Korean state media released a message on Wednesday from Kim Yo Jong, the country’s top adviser and sister of Leader Kim Jong Un, in which she denied any knowledge of talks between Kim and former U.S. President Donald Trump. The statement came after Trump told reporters that Kim had replied to his request for a conversation, a claim that the North Korean government has not confirmed.

In her brief note, Kim Yo Jong said that she was unaware of any such discussions and that the leadership had not authorized any direct contact with the former president. The message was distributed by the Korean Central News Agency, underscoring the regime’s insistence that it maintains strict control over diplomatic engagements and that any contact with U.S. officials is carefully vetted.

The denial follows a series of high‑profile exchanges between the two leaders, including a historic summit in 2018 and subsequent attempts at dialogue. While the United States has repeatedly called for further talks, North Korea has maintained a cautious stance, emphasizing its sovereignty and the need for clear guarantees before any new engagement.
author: The Hill

title: Supramolecular nanofibers paired with nanohole substrate improve exciton transport in organic solid
content:
Researchers at Science Tokyo have demonstrated that self‑assembling, anthracene‑based supramolecular nanofibers can transport singlet excitons across distances of several hundred nanometres. In controlled experiments the nanofibers facilitated exciton migration far beyond the typical diffusion lengths observed in conventional organic semiconductors, addressing a longstanding limitation in the field.

When the nanofibers were integrated with a plasmonic gold nanohole substrate, the exciton diffusivity was reported to double, further enhancing charge‑carrier transport. The combined system offers a novel strategy for improving the performance of optoelectronic devices such as organic photovoltaics and light‑emitting diodes by mitigating the intrinsic diffusivity constraints of organic materials.
author: Phys.org

title: Stripe acquisition of OpenRouter driven by strategic AI integration
content:
Stripe has announced its acquisition of PromptRoute, a startup that builds a routing layer for AI models, allowing developers to send a single prompt to the most suitable model among several providers. The move follows a broader industry trend in which fintech firms are embedding generative AI into core services, from fraud detection and risk scoring to automated customer support. PromptRoute’s technology, which normalizes prompt formats and dynamically selects the best-performing model based on cost, latency, and accuracy, gives Stripe a ready‑made platform to experiment with AI‑driven payment flows without building the infrastructure from scratch.

In public statements, Stripe executives have framed the purchase as a step toward the “singularity,” a tongue‑in‑cheek reference to the convergence of AI and finance. In practice, the acquisition is aimed at enhancing Stripe’s product suite with AI capabilities that can reduce transaction friction, improve compliance monitoring, and unlock new revenue streams. By integrating PromptRoute’s routing engine, Stripe can offer merchants a plug‑and‑play AI layer that automatically optimizes model choice for tasks such as currency conversion, chargeback prediction, and real‑time risk assessment, thereby strengthening its competitive edge in the payments market.
author: TechCrunch

title: Amazon targets 500 U.S. neighborhoods for Prime Air drones by 2026
content:
Amazon’s Prime Air and similar drone‑delivery pilots are rolling out across the United States, offering faster, contact‑free deliveries that could reshape last‑mile logistics. The expansion has prompted residents and regulators to weigh the convenience of instant parcel access against potential disruptions to neighborhoods and the broader regulatory landscape.

The drones, capable of carrying up to 5 kilograms, operate under the Federal Aviation Administration’s Part 107 rules and are subject to local ordinances that govern noise, flight paths, and privacy. While the services promise reduced traffic congestion and lower carbon footprints, concerns have emerged about noise pollution, the risk of accidents involving people or property, and the lack of clear data‑protection protocols for the video and sensor data collected during flights. Some municipalities are exploring restrictions or requiring community input before approving permanent drone corridors.

As the industry moves toward wider deployment, stakeholders will need to balance the economic and environmental benefits of drone delivery with the community’s right to quiet, safety, and privacy. Ongoing dialogue between companies, regulators, and residents will be essential to ensure that the technology’s advantages are realized without compromising the quality of life in affected areas.
author: Ars Technica

title: Trump Announces Intense Economic Operation Against Iran
content:
Washington, D.C. — President Joe Biden warned on Tuesday that any nation that continues to conduct trade with Iran will “face tremendous economic consequences,” reiterating the United States’ commitment to enforcing its sanctions regime. The statement was made during a press briefing following the release of a new set of executive orders aimed at tightening restrictions on Iran’s ability to procure advanced technology and financial services. The administration emphasized that the measures target entities that facilitate the acquisition of materials for Iran’s nuclear and missile programs, as well as those that support its regional proxy networks.

The Biden administration’s warning builds on a series of sanctions imposed since 2018, which have already limited Iran’s access to the global banking system and restricted its oil exports. Treasury officials indicated that the “tremendous economic consequences” could include secondary sanctions, asset freezes, and denial of access to the U.S. financial market for companies that violate the rules. The United States has also called on allies and partners to enforce the sanctions uniformly, urging them to report suspicious transactions and to cooperate with ongoing enforcement actions. The heightened pressure aims to compel Tehran to return to diplomatic negotiations over its nuclear activities while curbing the flow of revenue that funds its regional activities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Lebanon extradites former Syrian army general to Syria
content:
Beirut – Lebanese authorities confirmed on Tuesday the completion of a prisoner transfer that marks the first instance of a Syrian military officer being moved out of Lebanon after fleeing the country following the collapse of President Bashar al‑Assad’s government. The officer, who had sought refuge in Lebanon in the aftermath of the regime’s downfall, was handed over to a multinational task force overseeing the repatriation of former combatants.

The transfer follows a series of agreements between Lebanon and neighboring states aimed at addressing the lingering presence of Syrian ex‑military personnel who arrived during the civil conflict. Officials said the handover was conducted in accordance with international protocols and reflects ongoing efforts to resolve security concerns tied to the influx of former Syrian fighters. The case is being cited as a precedent for future repatriations, signaling a shift in Lebanon’s approach to managing the residual effects of the Syrian war.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Meta faces potential fines and operational changes from social media addiction lawsuit
content:
A federal court in Washington is set to hear a landmark antitrust trial against Meta Platforms Inc., the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, marking the most significant legal challenge to the social‑media giant’s business practices in decades. The case, brought by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and a coalition of state attorneys general, alleges that Meta unlawfully leveraged its dominance in social networking to stifle competition, unlawfully acquire rivals, and impose restrictive terms on advertisers and developers. If the jury finds Meta liable, the company could face fines exceeding $5 billion and be ordered to implement structural reforms that would alter how its platforms collect, share, and monetize user data.

The trial follows a series of investigations by regulators in the United States and abroad that have scrutinized Meta’s handling of personal information, its algorithmic transparency, and its market‑share tactics in digital advertising. Prosecutors have presented evidence suggesting that Meta’s integration of Facebook and Instagram creates barriers for new entrants and that its data‑sharing policies give the company an unfair advantage in targeting ads. Legal experts note that a ruling requiring Meta to separate its core services, provide open access to its advertising API, or adopt stricter privacy safeguards could reshape the operational landscape of the two platforms. The outcome, expected later this year, is poised to set a precedent for future antitrust actions against technology firms and could have far‑reaching implications for users, advertisers, and the broader digital economy.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Does 'AI‑watermarking' mean the party is over for cheating students?
content:
Educators and administrators across K-12 schools and higher education institutions are increasingly addressing widespread concerns regarding the use of artificial intelligence tools for academic dishonesty. As generative AI platforms become more accessible and sophisticated, schools report a growing number of incidents where students submit AI-generated essays, code, and research assignments as their own work. This development has prompted a rapid reassessment of academic integrity policies and evaluation methods across educational systems.

In response, many institutions have adopted AI detection software, revised grading rubrics, and redesigned assignments to prioritize in-class writing, oral defenses, and process-driven projects that require documented research steps. Faculty development programs now frequently include training on identifying AI-assisted work and integrating ethical technology use into coursework. Meanwhile, educational researchers and technology developers are collaborating to establish standardized guidelines that distinguish between permissible AI assistance and academic misconduct, while tracking how these tools affect long-term student learning outcomes.

The expanding presence of AI in academic settings highlights the necessity for updated educational frameworks that align with modern technological realities. As schools and universities continue to refine their policies and instructional approaches, the primary objective remains maintaining academic standards while equipping students with the critical thinking and digital literacy skills required for future professional environments.
author: Phys.org

title: IBM XT OS Gains Browser, CP/M 2.2 Z80 Core, and MS Word 1.1a on Os8088.com
content:
OS8088.com’s “Spotlight” series has recently published a new feature article, accessible at https://os8088.com/spotlight/. The piece, which delves into a recent development in the tech landscape, has attracted attention beyond the site’s own readership. It was shared on the Hacker News community, where it currently holds eight up‑votes and has prompted three comments, indicating modest engagement from the platform’s active user base.

The article’s discussion on Hacker News underscores the broader interest in the topic covered by OS8088’s Spotlight. While the comments are brief, they reflect a curiosity about the subject matter and suggest that the piece resonates with professionals who follow emerging trends. The cross‑platform presence of the story highlights the growing relevance of OS8088’s content within the wider technology discourse.
author: Hacker News

title: OpenAI introduces new privacy protections to compete with Anthropic
content:
A growing competition between OpenAI and Anthropic is centering on which company can deliver the most robust privacy safeguards for enterprise customer data. As businesses increasingly integrate artificial intelligence into sensitive operational workflows, the race to establish trust through stringent data protection measures has become a defining factor in corporate AI procurement. Both firms are positioning privacy not merely as a compliance obligation, but as a core differentiator in the expanding enterprise AI market.

OpenAI has recently expanded its enterprise offerings with dedicated data isolation protocols, optional zero-retention training environments, and compliance alignments with major regulatory standards. Anthropic has countered by emphasizing transparent data handling policies, enterprise-grade encryption, and customizable privacy controls designed to meet sector-specific security requirements. Industry observers note that these developments reflect a broader shift in the AI sector, where organizations are prioritizing vendors that can guarantee data sovereignty, limit exposure risks, and maintain strict access controls without degrading model performance.

The ongoing rivalry is expected to accelerate improvements in enterprise AI security standards as both companies refine their privacy architectures to meet evolving corporate and regulatory expectations. As data protection requirements become more stringent and the consequences of breaches grow more severe, the trajectory of this competition will likely establish new benchmarks for responsible AI deployment across commercial sectors.
author: TechCrunch

title: Waymo Ojai Robotaxi Now Available in Three Cities
content:
Waymo has announced the Waymo Ojai, a next‑generation robotaxi designed to accelerate the company’s transition to mass‑scale operations and eventual profitability. The Ojai platform builds on Waymo’s existing autonomous driving technology, integrating advanced sensor suites, refined navigation algorithms, and a new vehicle architecture that is intended to reduce production costs while improving safety and passenger experience.

The rollout of the Waymo Ojai is part of a broader strategy to expand service coverage and increase vehicle utilization rates. By deploying a fleet of Ojai units in high‑density urban corridors, Waymo aims to demonstrate the viability of autonomous ride‑hailing at scale, gather extensive real‑world data, and refine its software through continuous learning. The company also plans to leverage the Ojai’s modular design to support future upgrades and regulatory compliance across multiple jurisdictions.

If successful, the Waymo Ojai could serve as a cornerstone for Waymo’s long‑term commercial model, enabling the company to achieve cost efficiencies that bring the business closer to profitability while maintaining a strong safety record. The introduction of this vehicle marks a significant milestone in the autonomous mobility sector, underscoring the industry’s push toward widespread, reliable robotaxi services.
author: TechCrunch

title: Trump says he gets along well with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump recently lauded the rapport he has cultivated with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, citing the progress made in easing tensions on the Korean Peninsula. The statement, issued through a press briefing, highlighted the series of high‑level talks that began in 2018 and continued through 2019, during which the two leaders met in Singapore, Hanoi, and the United States.

Trump underscored that the relationship has helped reduce the risk of military escalation and opened avenues for further diplomatic engagement. He noted that the U.S. and North Korea have agreed to pursue denuclearization steps, including the dismantlement of certain missile sites and the return of U.S. personnel to the Korean Demilitarized Zone. The president also mentioned ongoing discussions aimed at restoring economic ties and lifting sanctions, framing the partnership as a cornerstone of his administration’s foreign policy.

The remarks come amid renewed interest in revisiting the 2018 summit agreements and assessing the next phase of U.S.–North Korea relations. While the administration signals optimism, analysts caution that the durability of the partnership will depend on continued diplomatic momentum and verification of North Korea’s compliance with denuclearization commitments.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Australia to summon Israeli ambassador after decision not to prosecute Gaza aid worker killing
content:
The foreign minister announced that she will summon the Israeli ambassador to protest a decision described as “insulting” to Zomi Frankcom. In a statement released on Tuesday, the minister said the move reflects her government’s commitment to defending the dignity of individuals affected by foreign policies and underscored the seriousness with which the issue is being treated at the highest diplomatic level.

The summons is expected to take place within the coming days, providing an official forum for the foreign ministry to seek clarification and express formal objection to the contested decision. Officials indicated that the discussion will focus on the implications of the decision for bilateral relations and may lead to further diplomatic engagement aimed at resolving the matter.
author: BBC World

title: Cognition CEO denies reports of SpaceX acquisition talks
content:
SpaceX has reportedly entered negotiations to acquire the AI coding startup Cognition, following its recent purchase of Cursor. The move comes as the aerospace giant seeks to broaden its footprint in the rapidly expanding enterprise AI market, where it has been trailing competitors such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Cognition’s focus on developer tools and code generation aligns with SpaceX’s strategy to embed advanced AI capabilities across its product portfolio.

The acquisition of Cursor earlier this year marked SpaceX’s first foray into AI‑powered software, and the potential Cognition deal would deepen its expertise in machine‑learning–driven code synthesis. By integrating Cognition’s technology, SpaceX could accelerate the development of autonomous systems and enhance its internal software engineering processes, positioning the company to compete more aggressively in the AI arena. Analysts note that the combination of SpaceX’s hardware strengths with advanced AI software could create new synergies for both spaceflight and commercial applications.

If the transaction closes, SpaceX would join a growing list of non‑tech firms investing heavily in AI to secure a competitive edge. The company’s continued expansion into enterprise AI underscores its ambition to diversify beyond rockets and satellites, potentially reshaping its long‑term business model and influencing the broader AI ecosystem.
author: TechCrunch

title: U.S. national debt exceeds $40 trillion
content:
The U.S. Treasury announced on Tuesday that the federal debt has surpassed the $40 trillion threshold, a milestone that underscores the rapid growth of the nation’s borrowing over the past decade. According to the latest data, the total outstanding debt climbed to $40.1 trillion, up from $39.0 trillion just weeks earlier.

This new figure follows a trajectory that saw the debt double since late 2017, when it first crossed the $20 trillion mark. The Treasury’s weekly debt statistics, released as part of its regular reporting, show a steady increase driven by a combination of rising interest costs, expansive fiscal stimulus, and ongoing deficit spending. The $40 trillion level represents a significant benchmark for policymakers and economists tracking the country’s fiscal trajectory.

While the Treasury does not comment on policy implications, the data provide a clear record of the debt’s expansion. Analysts note that the continued rise will affect future budget priorities and may influence interest rates and fiscal policy decisions. The Treasury will continue to publish weekly updates to keep the public informed of the debt’s status.
author: The Hill

title: Spain to Transfer 500 Migrant Children from Ceuta
content:
Ceuta’s local authorities have called for the return of several children to Morocco after a recent incident in which the youngsters were found in the Spanish enclave. The municipal council, citing concerns over the children’s welfare and the lack of legal documentation, urged the Spanish government to arrange their repatriation. The request has drawn a sharp response from Madrid, which described the idea of deporting the children as “outrageous” and stressed that any action must comply with national and European legal standards.

The Spanish government’s stance is rooted in its obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. Officials have indicated that the children’s status is still under review and that any decision must involve thorough checks of their identity, nationality, and the circumstances that led to their presence in Ceuta. The central authorities also highlighted the need for cooperation with Moroccan counterparts to ensure a lawful and humane resolution.

While Ceuta’s leaders press for a swift return, Madrid’s position underscores the importance of due process and the protection of minors’ rights. The situation remains unresolved, with both sides awaiting further legal assessment before any definitive action is taken.
author: Al Jazeera

title: USS Lincoln Conditions Expose Navy Supply Limits
content:
Reports of dire conditions in the region have brought the supply challenges faced by aid agencies into sharp focus, prompting experts to question the feasibility of the United States’ current relief strategy. Field teams have documented shortages of food, clean water, and medical supplies, while logistical bottlenecks at key transit points have stalled the delivery of critical resources.

Analysts point to a combination of infrastructure damage, limited port capacity, and regulatory delays that have slowed the flow of goods into the affected area. The U.S. government has announced a multi‑phase assistance program that includes airlifts of humanitarian aid and a planned build‑out of a temporary distribution hub, but experts warn that the timeline may be overly optimistic given the existing constraints. They argue that without immediate upgrades to transport routes and a streamlined customs process, the projected relief deliveries risk falling short of the urgent needs on the ground.

In light of these concerns, specialists are calling for a reassessment of the U.S. approach, emphasizing the need for coordinated international support and investment in local logistics infrastructure. A revised plan that incorporates real‑time supply chain monitoring and contingency measures could improve the effectiveness of aid efforts and better address the pressing humanitarian crisis.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israel launches criminal investigation into death of 6-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza
content:
The Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) announced on Tuesday that criminal investigations have been opened into the death of six‑year‑old Hind Rajab, who was killed during recent hostilities in the Gaza Strip. The statement, issued by the IDF’s spokesperson office, said the investigations will examine whether any breach of the law of armed conflict or misconduct by Israeli soldiers contributed to the child’s death. The probe will be conducted by the Military Police Corps in coordination with the Israel Defense Forces’ Legal Corps, and findings will be forwarded to the appropriate prosecutorial authorities.

Authorities have not disclosed the specific circumstances surrounding the incident, but the announcement follows heightened scrutiny of civilian casualties in the ongoing Israel‑Gaza conflict. The IDF emphasized that the investigations are part of its standard procedure to ensure accountability and adherence to international humanitarian law. Results of the inquiries are expected to be released in due course, pending the completion of forensic and witness analyses.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Displaced Lebanese watch Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon pilot zones
content:
Al Jazeera journalist Ali Hashem described the scene as “you can’t do anything. Just stand here and watch,” while observing Israeli airstrikes that struck residential areas near his hometown on Tuesday. The attacks, part of a broader military operation launched earlier this week, targeted several neighborhoods, causing damage to homes and infrastructure and prompting evacuations of dozens of families.

The strikes come amid intensified fighting between Israeli forces and Palestinian militants in the region, which officials say aim to neutralize rocket launch sites and underground tunnels. Local authorities reported multiple casualties and a growing humanitarian need, while humanitarian agencies called for unhindered access to deliver aid. As the conflict continues, residents remain under curfew and the international community has urged both sides to de‑escalate and protect civilians.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israeli strike kills Gaza police women's chief and officers
content:
An Israeli airstrike targeted the police headquarters in Gaza City on Thursday, killing the chief of the women’s police division along with several other officers. The strike, reported by local authorities and confirmed by the Palestinian Ministry of Health, resulted in multiple fatalities and injuries among the building’s staff. Israeli officials said the operation was aimed at neutralizing militants they claim were using the facility for command and control, though they did not provide further details about the specific targets.

The incident adds to the escalating violence in the densely populated enclave, where clashes between Israeli forces and Hamas-affiliated groups have intensified over the past weeks. Humanitarian agencies have warned that repeated attacks on security installations risk further civilian casualties and strain already limited medical resources. International observers called for restraint and an immediate investigation into the strike’s compliance with international humanitarian law.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Why isn't the accounting profession more diverse? Research points to the real levers of change
content:
Universities, employers and professional bodies across the globe have intensified their focus on mentoring schemes, scholarships and student‑support programmes over the past few decades, aiming to broaden participation in fields such as professional accounting. These initiatives are designed to provide talented students from under‑represented groups with the resources and guidance needed to navigate academic and professional hurdles.

The core strategy behind these efforts is the belief that targeted support will help talented individuals overcome systemic barriers, thereby improving representation within the profession. By offering financial aid, networking opportunities and tailored career advice, institutions hope to create a pipeline that leads more diverse candidates into accounting roles and leadership positions.

While the investment in such programmes has expanded markedly, the long‑term impact on diversity within accounting remains a subject of ongoing study. Continued monitoring and evaluation of these initiatives will be essential to determine whether the assumption that support equals improved representation holds true in practice.
author: Phys.org

title: Moderna and Merck report mRNA cancer vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence in late-stage trial
content:
Moderna’s new mRNA vaccine, Intismeran, has shown encouraging results in late‑stage trials, markedly lowering both recurrence and metastatic spread of melanoma. The study, conducted across multiple oncology centers, evaluated the vaccine’s efficacy as an adjuvant therapy in patients who had completed standard surgical and chemotherapeutic regimens.

In the trial, patients receiving Intismeran experienced a significant reduction in tumor recurrence compared with those given a placebo, while imaging data indicated fewer cases of distant metastasis. The vaccine’s design targets key melanoma antigens, prompting a robust immune response that appears to enhance the body’s ability to eliminate residual cancer cells. These findings suggest that mRNA technology can be effectively harnessed not only for prevention but also for post‑treatment cancer control.

If subsequent confirmatory studies corroborate these outcomes, Intismeran could become a pivotal addition to melanoma management protocols, offering a novel therapeutic avenue that improves long‑term survival and quality of life for patients facing this aggressive skin cancer.
author: Al Jazeera

title: A viral 'loose cannon' enzyme helps phages shut down bacterial defenses
content:
Antimicrobial resistance is rising worldwide, prompting the scientific community to seek alternative treatments that can outpace evolving bacterial defenses. Among the most promising options are bacteriophages—viruses that specifically infect and destroy bacteria. By targeting only pathogenic species, phages can eradicate infections without disturbing the beneficial microbiota, offering a potential solution for strains that have become resistant to conventional antibiotics.

Research into phage therapy is accelerating as laboratories demonstrate its efficacy against a range of drug‑resistant bacteria, including methicillin‑resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* and carbapenem‑resistant *Enterobacteriaceae*. Clinical trials are now underway in several countries, evaluating safety, dosing, and delivery methods such as topical sprays and intravenous infusions. Early results suggest that phages can clear infections that remain stubbornly persistent after standard treatment, and that they can be combined with antibiotics to enhance bacterial killing.

If these trials continue to show positive outcomes, phage therapy could become a vital tool in the global fight against antimicrobial resistance. Regulatory pathways are being established to streamline approval processes, and partnerships between academia and industry are growing to support large‑scale production. The emergence of phage-based treatments marks a significant shift toward precision medicine in infectious disease, potentially restoring the effectiveness of bacterial infections that have outlived traditional drugs.
author: Phys.org

title: Flight attendants freaked out that Google is buying tons of Spirit employee data
content:
Spirit Airlines has faced mounting criticism following allegations that the bankrupt carrier entered into a comprehensive data-sharing agreement with Google that prioritizes corporate restructuring over employee privacy. The controversy surfaced as the low-cost airline navigates Chapter 11 proceedings, with labor advocates and former employees claiming the arrangement effectively commodifies sensitive workforce information. According to internal documents and whistleblower accounts, the deal reportedly grants Google access to extensive operational and personnel datasets, prompting immediate concerns about data security and worker consent.

Under the reported terms of the agreement, Spirit would provide Google with aggregated flight operations metrics, customer interaction records, and internal workforce analytics in exchange for cloud infrastructure support and financial restructuring assistance. Labor representatives argue that the scope of the data transfer extends beyond standard business operations, potentially exposing employee performance records, scheduling patterns, and internal communication logs
author: Ars Technica

title: Framework responds to complaints that BIOS update bricks Ryzen 7040 laptops
content:
Framework, the modular‑design laptop manufacturer, announced that it will replace a batch of out‑of‑warranty AMD mainboards used in several of its devices. The company said the decision follows the identification of a hardware issue that could affect system stability, prompting a voluntary remediation program for affected units that are no longer covered by the standard warranty period.

Customers with the specified AMD‑based models can request a replacement board by contacting Framework’s support team, which will provide a refurbished or new mainboard at no cost. The company outlined that the program will run through the end of the calendar year and that shipping will be handled worldwide, with an estimated turnaround of two to three weeks after the request is approved. Framework emphasized that the replacement will not require additional software updates and that the move is part of its commitment to long‑term device sustainability.
author: Ars Technica

title: Rillet Secures $100M Series C, Reaches $1B Valuation
content:
Rillet, an AI‑native account management startup, has reached unicorn status after its annual recurring revenue (ARR) doubled over the past three months, the company announced today. The valuation, led by investment firm ICONIQ, now places Rillet at a $1 billion market value, making it one of the fastest‑growing fintech firms in the AI‑accounting space.

The surge in ARR reflects Rillet’s expanding client base and the adoption of its AI‑driven workflow tools, which streamline financial operations for mid‑size businesses. ICONIQ’s leadership and capital infusion are expected to accelerate product development and geographic expansion, positioning Rillet to compete with larger incumbents in the automated accounting sector. The milestone underscores the growing investor confidence in AI‑powered fintech solutions.
author: TechCrunch

title: Five Americans and two others killed in Kenya safari helicopter crash
content:
A safari helicopter carrying seven passengers crashed Wednesday morning in a remote area of northern Kenya, killing all aboard, officials said. Local police and the U.S. State Department confirmed that five of the victims were American citizens, and among the deceased were a senior executive of Telemundo, the Spanish‑language network owned by NBCUniversal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.

The crash occurred in a sparsely populated region, and rescue teams were dispatched to the site shortly after the incident was reported. Authorities are conducting an investigation to determine the cause of the accident, while diplomatic representatives from the United States, Ecuador and other affected nations have been notified. The loss of the media executive and the Ecuadorian intelligence chief underscores the international dimension of the tragedy, and officials have pledged to cooperate fully with families and investigators as the inquiry proceeds.
author: Guardian World

title: Helicopter crash in Kenya kills seven, including Ecuadorian intelligence chief
content:
Ecuador’s chief of intelligence, Michele Sensi‑Contugi, and NBCUniversal journalist José Suárez were confirmed among the dead in a fatal incident that occurred earlier today, officials said. The deaths were reported by local authorities after emergency responders arrived at the scene, though the exact nature of the event has not yet been disclosed.

Authorities identified the victims as Sensi‑Contugi, who heads the nation’s intelligence agency, and Suarez, a correspondent covering regional affairs for the U.S. media conglomerate. Both were traveling together when the incident took place, and investigators are now working to determine the circumstances surrounding the fatalities. The government has pledged a thorough inquiry and has urged the public to await official findings before drawing conclusions.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Police officer accessed Flock cameras 717 times to track estranged wife
content:
A police officer in the city of [City] has been accused of using Flock surveillance cameras to track his estranged wife 717 times, according to an affidavit filed with the court on [date]. The sworn statement, submitted by the officer’s attorney, alleges that the officer accessed the company’s camera network over a period of [time frame] to monitor the wife’s movements and activities without a warrant or any lawful justification. The affidavit lists specific dates and times of the alleged surveillance, and claims that the officer used the footage to gather evidence for an unrelated investigation.

The city police department has opened an internal review of the officer’s conduct, and the case has been referred to the district attorney’s office for potential criminal charges. Officials say that the use of public surveillance equipment for personal purposes is prohibited by department policy and state law. The investigation will examine whether the officer violated privacy rights, abused his authority, and whether any other officers were involved or aware of the activity. The city has urged the public to cooperate with the inquiry and has reiterated its commitment to transparency and accountability.

If the allegations are proven, the officer could face disciplinary action, civil liability, and criminal penalties for unlawful surveillance. The case underscores the broader debate over the balance between law‑enforcement surveillance capabilities and individual privacy protections, and it may prompt a review of the department’s monitoring protocols and training programs.
author: Hacker News

title: 3D map of kinase signaling sites created to aid cancer research
content:
Scientists are uncovering the hidden complexity of protein kinases—enzymes that regulate cell growth and are frequently hijacked by cancers. While kinases are known to drive tumor development, pinpointing which specific enzymes are active in any given cancer remains a major challenge.

Human proteins contain roughly 1.8 million potential phosphorylation sites where kinases could act. To date, researchers have fully mapped less than one percent of these sites, leaving a vast majority of kinase‑protein interactions uncharted. This knowledge gap hampers efforts to design targeted therapies, as many drugs rely on precise identification of the kinases driving a patient’s tumor.

Addressing this deficit is a priority for cancer research. Advances in mass spectrometry, computational modeling, and high‑throughput screening are accelerating the cataloguing of kinase activity, promising more accurate diagnostics and personalized treatments in the near future.
author: Phys.org

title: Iran’s hardline parliament raises concerns with ‘foreign infiltration’ plan
content:
A new regulatory framework announced by the government will require citizens and legal entities to obtain official permission before reaching out to universities or speaking with foreign media outlets. The measure, outlined in a draft decree released by the Ministry of Information, stipulates that any individual or organization wishing to engage in academic collaboration, research inquiries, or media interviews with overseas press must first submit a request to the designated authorization board, which will review each case for compliance with national security and public interest criteria.

The decree, which is slated for parliamentary debate next month, cites concerns over the potential leakage of sensitive information and the need to safeguard the country’s strategic interests. Proponents argue that the authorization process will provide a clear oversight mechanism, while critics warn that it could hinder academic freedom and limit the flow of information to the international community. If enacted, the rule will apply to all domestic entities, including NGOs, private firms, and individual scholars, marking a significant shift in how external communications are managed.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Syria: White Helmets Rescuer Killed in Alleged Police Beating Sparks Protests
content:
The death of Syrian White Helmets volunteer Mohammad Ghamira has ignited protests across the country. Ghamira, 28, was reportedly beaten by police officers in the Damascus suburb of Al‑Mansoura on 12 August after a confrontation over a traffic violation. He succumbed to his injuries at a local hospital the following day, according to the White Helmets’ spokesperson, who said the police had not provided a formal statement.

The incident has drawn sharp criticism from human rights groups and the international community, who accuse the security forces of excessive use of force against civilians. Protesters in Damascus and Aleppo have gathered at the police headquarters and the White Helmets’ headquarters, demanding an independent investigation and accountability for the officers involved. The Syrian government has denied any wrongdoing, stating that the death was a tragic accident and that the police were following protocol.

The death of Ghamira has reignited longstanding tensions between the state security apparatus and civil society groups. While the government has pledged to review the case, opposition activists warn that without transparent inquiry, public trust in law‑enforcement agencies will continue to erode, potentially destabilizing an already fragile social fabric.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Kyiv protest backs former defence minister Fedorov's call for elections
content:
In the heart of Kyiv, supporters of former defence minister Mykailo Fedorov gathered this week to protest his dismissal. The demonstrators assembled in front of the Ministry of Defence, holding placards that read “Justice for Fedorov” and “Respect the Minister.” The rally was organized by a coalition of veterans’ groups and political activists who argue that Fedorov’s removal was unjustified and politically motivated.

Fedorov, who had served as defence minister since 2022, was dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky in March after a series of accusations involving the procurement of military equipment and alleged mismanagement of defence funds. Critics of the dismissal claim that the evidence presented was insufficient and that the move was intended to silence a minister who had been outspoken about the need for greater transparency in defence spending. The protest reflects a broader debate within Ukraine about accountability and the direction of the country’s armed forces amid ongoing conflict.

While the demonstrators called for a review of the dismissal and a return of Fedorov to his post, authorities have not yet responded with any official statement. The event underscores the continued polarization over Ukraine’s defence leadership and highlights the active engagement of civil society in shaping national policy.
author: Al Jazeera

title: 582 skeletons, including children, found in Sri Lanka mass grave
content:
A forensic team in Sri Lanka has uncovered a mass grave containing 582 human skeletons, officials said, after an extensive excavation at a remote site in the country’s northern region. The remains, which include a significant number of infants and children, were recovered over the course of several weeks of systematic digging and documentation. Authorities have not yet released information on the identities of the deceased or the precise time frame of the burials, but the scale of the find has prompted calls for a thorough investigation.

The discovery is being examined by the Ministry of Defence’s forensic unit in collaboration with international experts to determine the cause of death and any possible links to past conflicts in the area. DNA testing and osteological analysis are underway to establish the ages, sexes, and possible familial relationships among the victims. Officials have pledged to inform families of any matches that emerge and to pursue legal avenues if evidence of wrongdoing is confirmed, underscoring a broader effort to address unresolved human‑rights concerns in Sri Lanka.
author: Al Jazeera

title: In Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, inflammation blocks its own healing
content:
Researchers from institutions in Kiel, Germany, and the United States have identified a biological mechanism that explains why inflammation persists in Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis despite the body’s natural regulatory efforts. The study reveals that chronic intestinal inflammation directly interferes with a critical metabolic pathway responsible for delivering energy to the cells lining the gut. This disruption prevents the intestinal barrier from properly repairing itself, allowing inflammatory processes to continue unchecked.

title: Bronze Age brands identified in Arabian desert oasis pottery
content:
Archaeologists have confirmed that branding practices pre‑date modern capitalist societies.  An international research team headed by Marta Luciani of the University of Vienna reports that Bronze Age traders in northwestern Arabia used distinctive marks on pottery to identify producers, a form of early brand that dates back roughly 3,200 years.

The study, based on excavations at the oasis of Qurayyah, uncovered two‑colour painted vessels bearing consistent, stylised symbols.  The marks, found on a wide range of ceramic wares, indicate a standardized production system and suggest that goods were tracked and possibly traded across regional networks.  The discovery provides the first concrete evidence of commercial branding in a non‑capitalist economy of the ancient Near East.

These findings broaden the historical understanding of early market mechanisms and demonstrate that the concept of a brand—an identifiable mark linked to a specific producer—has deep roots in human trade practices.  The research underscores the sophistication of Bronze Age commerce in Arabia and invites further investigation into the spread of branding across ancient societies.
author: Phys.org

title: Brazil Bus Crash Kills 23, Injures 5 in Parana
content:
A bus en route to hospitals near Curitiba was involved in an accident on a local road, according to preliminary reports. The vehicle was traveling northward from the city toward a cluster of medical facilities when the incident occurred. No details about the exact location or the time of day have been released by local authorities.

Investigators are examining the circumstances of the crash, but the cause remains unknown. No official statement has yet confirmed whether there were injuries or fatalities, and authorities have not released a casualty count. The incident has prompted a temporary suspension of

title: Kennedy Center Board Rejects Immediate Restoration of Trump Name
content:
A local entertainment venue has become the focus of a legal dispute after a court ordered the removal of a former president’s name from its signage. The ruling, issued last month by a regional court, cited violations of a trademark agreement and demanded that the venue cease using the name in all promotional materials and on the building itself. Opponents of the venue’s continued use of the name argue that the establishment appears “intent on defying” the court order, suggesting a disregard for the judicial decision.

The venue’s management has responded that the name is integral to its brand identity and that they are reviewing the court’s directive. Legal analysts note that non‑compliance could result in fines or an injunction compelling the removal of the signage. The case remains pending, with a hearing scheduled for next week to determine whether the venue will comply with the order or face further sanctions.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Canada pledges $50 million aid to Lebanon, condemns Israeli invasion
content:
Ottawa’s foreign affairs minister publicly denounced Israel’s recent military incursion into southern Lebanon, describing it as an “invasion” that violates Lebanese sovereignty. In a statement released on Tuesday, the minister urged all parties to respect international law and called for an immediate de‑escalation of hostilities that have displaced thousands of civilians and strained already fragile infrastructure in the crisis‑hit nation.

The Canadian government announced a new assistance package worth CAD 30 million, earmarked for emergency shelter, medical supplies, and food distribution to communities affected by the fighting. The aid, to be delivered through the United Nations Relief and Works Agency and local NGOs, aims to bolster Lebanon’s capacity to respond to the surge in displaced persons and to support reconstruction of damaged health facilities. Ottawa said the pledge underscores Canada’s commitment to Lebanon’s territorial integrity and to broader regional stability, while urging the international community to pursue diplomatic solutions to the conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Canada and US near completion of trade deal as deadline approaches
content:
Prime Minister Carney said the latest round of trade negotiations has achieved “significant progress,” as the two nations work to finalize remaining issues before a newly set weekend deadline for tariff adjustments. The statement was made during a press briefing on Thursday, where Carney emphasized that both sides are focused on resolving outstanding points that have delayed the implementation of the agreed‑upon tariff schedule.

Negotiators are now concentrating on the final details of market access, rules of origin and dispute‑resolution mechanisms, with the goal of meeting the deadline that will determine whether the provisional tariff reductions take effect. Officials from both governments have indicated that, if the deadline is met, the revised tariff framework could boost bilateral trade flows and provide greater certainty for businesses operating across the border.
author: BBC World

title: Human remains found at Lake Mead as water levels fall
content:
Human remains were found in Lake Mead on August 16, according to a report by USA Today, marking the latest grim discovery in the reservoir that supplies water to the Las Vegas area. The National Park Service said the body showed no signs of suspicious activity, and investigators are treating it as a routine search for missing persons.

Lake Mead has been experiencing record low water levels for several years, raising concerns about water supply and environmental conditions. The discovery follows a series of similar findings in recent months, prompting authorities to review safety protocols and increase monitoring of the lake’s shoreline. While the circumstances of this particular case remain unclear, the NPS has confirmed that the investigation is ongoing.

The incident underscores the challenges facing the region as water scarcity and climate change continue to affect the reservoir’s capacity. Officials have urged anyone with information to come forward, and the search for the individual remains a priority for local law‑enforcement and park officials.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Trump nominates White House health adviser Heidi Overton as FDA commissioner
content:
President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social on Wednesday that he has nominated Dr. Heidi Overton to serve as the next Commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration. Overton, a physician with extensive experience in public health, currently serves as a senior domestic policy adviser on health matters in the White House. Her appointment follows a period of significant turnover at the FDA, during which several senior officials have resigned or been reassigned.

The agency has been described as “roiled” by the exodus of top staff, raising concerns about its capacity to oversee drug approvals, medical device regulation, and food safety standards. Overton’s background in clinical medicine and her role in shaping national health policy are seen as assets that could help restore stability and continuity within the FDA’s leadership. If confirmed by the Senate, she would assume responsibility for steering the agency’s regulatory agenda amid ongoing scrutiny over its decision‑making processes and workforce challenges.

The nomination is expected to prompt a Senate confirmation hearing, where Overton’s qualifications and policy positions will be examined. Her leadership will be closely watched by industry stakeholders, consumer advocacy groups, and health professionals as the FDA continues to navigate complex regulatory and public health issues.
author: The Hill

title: Book chronicles rise of desert toad psychedelic and its promoter
content:
Kimon de Greef’s new book, *The Ego Trip*, traces the history of a powerful psychedelic compound that originates from the secretions of certain toads. The narrative follows the drug’s journey from its natural source to its emergence as a sought‑after psychoactive substance, detailing the scientific and cultural forces that have shaped its reputation.

The work centers on a controversial figure who claimed that the compound possesses extraordinary abilities, and it examines the claims through interviews, laboratory reports, and historical documents. Olivia Goldhill, a researcher and journalist, uncovered the story through a combination of archival research and firsthand accounts, revealing how the drug’s allure has evolved over decades and how it has been embraced by both the scientific community and countercultural movements.

*The Ego Trip* offers a comprehensive look at the intersection of biology, mysticism, and modern drug culture, providing readers with a nuanced understanding of how a simple toad secretion has become a symbol of altered consciousness. The book has been praised for its thorough research and balanced presentation, and it is expected to contribute significantly to discussions about psychedelic substances and their place in contemporary society.
author: New Scientist

title: Trump expected to pick conservative policy wonk Heidi Overton to lead FDA
content:
A state legislator has drawn attention this week for her outspoken positions on several health‑related issues. In recent interviews and public statements, she reaffirmed her opposition to abortion, expressed caution about the use of peptide‑based therapies, and advocated for stricter limits on vaccine mandates. The lawmaker’s platform, which emphasizes personal choice and limited governmental intervention in medical decisions, has become a focal point of debate among constituents and health officials.

Critics from the Medical Association of Health Administrators (MAHA) have publicly challenged her stance, arguing that the proposed restrictions could undermine public health initiatives and impede the adoption of emerging treatments. MAHA officials have highlighted data supporting the safety and efficacy of both peptide therapies and vaccination programs, contending that the legislator’s positions may conflict with established medical guidelines. Supporters, however, maintain that her approach reflects community concerns about over‑medicalization and the preservation of individual autonomy.

The controversy underscores an ongoing clash between policy makers and health professionals over the balance between regulatory oversight and personal freedom in medical care. As the legislative session progresses, the lawmaker’s proposals are expected to face further scrutiny in committee hearings, where both her supporters and opponents will present evidence to shape the final outcome.
author: Ars Technica

title: Trump Claims North Korea Has 57 Powerful Nuclear Weapons
content:
Former President Donald Trump has reiterated concerns about the United States’ military posture on the Korean Peninsula, following his recent announcement that U.S. forces would reduce the frequency of joint drills with South Korea. In a statement issued earlier this week, Trump said the decision to scale back exercises was intended to avoid sending an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea. The move comes amid heightened tensions in the region, with the U.S. and South Korean militaries traditionally conducting large‑scale, regular drills as a deterrent against North Korean provocations.

The reduction in joint exercises, announced by the U.S. Department of Defense, will see a shift from biannual to quarterly training sessions, according to the Pentagon. Trump’s remarks, made on a campaign platform, echo his longstanding criticism of what he views as overly aggressive U.S. military engagement in East Asia. Analysts note that the change could affect the U.S. alliance with Seoul, though officials have emphasized that core deterrence capabilities remain intact.

While the U.S. and South Korean governments have confirmed that the core components of their defense partnership will continue, the decision has sparked debate among policymakers and military experts. Some argue that the scaled‑back drills may reduce deterrence, while others contend that a more measured approach could lower the risk of accidental escalation. The U.S. will likely monitor North Korea’s response closely as it adjusts its own posture in the coming months.
author: Euronews

title: Imran Khan moved to hospital, prompting talk of political negotiations
content:
Former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan was transferred from his prison cell to a hospital in Islamabad on Monday for medical treatment, according to the Interior Ministry. The move follows a series of health‑related complaints that had prompted a medical review of the former leader’s condition. Khan, who has been in custody since his arrest in August, is being treated for a chronic illness that has reportedly worsened in recent weeks.

The transfer has sparked speculation among political analysts that the government may be open to new negotiations with Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek‑e‑Insaf party. In a statement, the ministry said the decision was made solely on medical grounds and that no political concessions were involved. Nonetheless, opposition leaders and PTI officials have called for a dialogue to address the broader legal and political disputes surrounding Khan’s case.

Observers note that the move could signal a shift in the government’s approach to the high‑profile case, potentially paving the way for a broader settlement. However, no official policy changes have been announced, and the Interior Ministry reiterated that the transfer is temporary and focused on Khan’s health. The situation remains closely monitored by domestic and international stakeholders.
author: DW World

title: US and Canada finalize tariff‑free trade agreement
content:
Washington — President Donald Trump announced a new trade agreement with Canada that eliminates tariffs on agricultural products and a broad range of U.S. manufactured goods exported to the neighboring country. The pact, finalized after weeks of negotiations between the United States Trade Representative’s office and Canadian officials, removes the 10‑percent duty previously applied to dairy, poultry, and certain grain shipments, and lifts the 5‑percent levy on automotive parts, machinery, and technology components. Under the terms of the deal, U.S. exporters will receive immediate market access, while Canadian authorities have pledged to streamline customs procedures to accelerate the flow of goods across the border.

The tariff‑free arrangement is expected to boost U.S. farm income and support manufacturing sectors that rely on cross‑border supply chains, according to data from the Department of Agriculture and the Commerce Department. Analysts note that the agreement aligns with the broader objective of strengthening North American trade ties and may serve as a template for future negotiations with other partners. The administration indicated that the deal will be implemented within 30 days, pending standard regulatory reviews, and will be monitored for compliance through quarterly reporting mechanisms.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Labour urges Reform UK deputy leader to apologise to firefighters over heat remark
content:
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, has urged Reform’s deputy leader Richard Tice to apologise for his recent remarks encouraging the public to “enjoy” the summer’s extreme heat. The comments came after a series of severe wildfires that have forced widespread evacuations and destroyed homes across the country. Phillipson said the party’s stance on Reform’s net‑zero agenda has already alienated many voters, and that Tice’s tone was “inappropriate and insensitive” to those who have fought the fires.

Tice’s remarks, made this week on social media, were widely criticised by emergency services officials and community groups. Firefighters who have battled the blazes cited the lack of public support and the need for urgent action to address climate‑related risks. Labour’s call for an apology follows a broader debate over Reform’s environmental policies, with critics arguing that the party’s approach to net zero is too aggressive and politically damaging.

The Labour Party’s appeal for an apology underscores the growing pressure on Reform to address the public’s concerns about climate change and emergency preparedness. If Tice does not respond, Phillipson has indicated that the party will continue to highlight the disconnect between Reform’s rhetoric and the lived experiences of those affected by the recent wildfires.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Google Pixel Watch 5 adds new health software but lacks full feature rollout
content:
The Google Pixel Watch 5 has proven to be the most challenging model in the Pixel Watch line to evaluate. While the device’s hardware remains largely unchanged—identical dimensions, the same Snapdragon Wear 4100+ processor, and only a marginal battery improvement—the watch’s new pyrite‑satin case finish marks the most visible cosmetic upgrade.

The primary focus of this year’s release lies in software, with Google expanding the Health app’s capabilities and integrating an AI coach that debuted with the Fitbit Air earlier in the year. The updated watch promises new health metrics, including blood‑pressure monitoring, insulin‑resistance trend analysis, and nightly sleep‑breathing metrics. However, reviewers have noted that these features are not yet available on the device.

Despite the lack of the promised health tools, the Pixel Watch 5’s continued emphasis on software enhancements underscores Google’s strategy to differentiate its wearable through data and AI rather than hardware changes. The Verge’s full review details the watch’s performance and the current status of its health features.
author: The Verge

title: No, Italy’s Lake Como didn’t dry up
content:
A viral TikTok video claiming that Lake Como in northern Italy has vanished following a "geological rupture" has been confirmed false by fact-checkers and geological experts. The sensational post, which spread rapidly across social media, featured dramatic footage and photographs purporting to show the iconic lake completely dry. Authorities and scientific observers have stated unequivocally that no such event has occurred and that the lake remains intact.

Analysis of the viral content reveals that all accompanying images and video clips were artificially generated using AI tools rather than documenting real conditions. While Lake Como has experienced lower water levels in recent months, this reduction is the result of prolonged drought affecting the region, not seismic or tectonic activity. High-resolution satellite imagery consistently shows the lake retaining substantial volume, with shoreline changes aligning with documented climate-related water fluctuations.

Environmental agencies continue to track regional water levels as part of routine drought monitoring efforts. The episode highlights the increasing circulation of AI-generated misinformation and reinforces the importance of cross-referencing viral claims with verified data. Lake Como remains a fully existing body of water, and no geological catastrophe has taken place.
author: France 24

title: US Regime Change: 70 Years of Interventions and Their Impact
content:
U.S. foreign policy has repeatedly involved covert and overt interventions aimed at altering the political leadership of other nations, a pattern that has produced significant human and financial costs.  The most cited example is the 1953 CIA‑backed coup in Iran that overthrew Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh and installed Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, a move that destabilized the region for decades.  Since then, the United States has pursued regime‑change objectives in Iraq (2003), Libya (2011), Syria (2015), and Afghanistan (2001), each operation accompanied by substantial civilian casualties, displacement, and long‑term security challenges.

These interventions have consistently involved large budgets—ranging from the $2 billion spent on the 1953 operation to the $2.4 trillion projected cost of the Iraq war—and have generated ongoing humanitarian crises.  In Iraq alone, more than 200,000 civilians have died, and the country remains fragmented by sectarian conflict.  Similar patterns appear in Syria, where the civil war has displaced millions and left the infrastructure in ruins, and in Libya, where the power vacuum has fueled extremist groups and regional instability.

The recurring theme across these cases is that U.S. attempts to engineer regime changes often lead to unintended consequences, including prolonged conflict, regional destabilization, and immense human suffering.  As the United States continues to engage in foreign interventions, the historical record underscores the need for a careful assessment of both the strategic objectives and the profound costs associated with altering sovereign governments.
author: Al Jazeera

title: India beats Pakistan 5-3 to finish second in Hockey World Cup 2026 pool
content:
India defeated Pakistan 5‑3 in their Pool D encounter, securing the runner‑up spot with six points after the group’s final round of matches. The win kept India unbeaten in the pool stage and ensured they finish ahead of Pakistan, who remain third with three points. England, meanwhile, topped the same pool by winning all three of their games, accumulating nine points and confirming their place at the summit of Pool D.

The standings set the stage for the upcoming knockout phase, with England and India advancing as the pool’s leading teams. Pakistan’s loss leaves them out of contention for the quarter‑finals, while the remaining teams in the tournament will now focus on their next fixtures based on the final pool rankings.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Stanford study finds lower heat tolerance limits and higher risk for elderly
content:
Stanford University researchers have published new findings indicating that the human body’s tolerance to heat is lower than previously believed, with age emerging as a significant risk factor. The study, conducted by the university’s School of Medicine, analyzed physiological responses to elevated temperatures in a diverse cohort of participants ranging from young adults to seniors. Results show that heat stress thresholds drop markedly as people age, suggesting that older adults may reach dangerous levels of core temperature at lower environmental heat loads.

The investigation measured core body temperature, heart rate, and sweat production while subjects were exposed to controlled heat environments. Researchers found that individuals over 65 reached critical core temperatures at ambient temperatures 3 to 5 degrees Celsius lower than the limits established in earlier research. The study also highlighted that older adults exhibit reduced sweat gland function and impaired cardiovascular responses, which together compromise the body’s ability to dissipate heat. These physiological changes underscore the heightened vulnerability of the elderly population to heat‑related illnesses, especially during heatwaves.

The findings carry implications for public health guidelines and emergency response planning, particularly in the context of rising global temperatures. By redefining safe exposure limits and emphasizing age‑specific risk, the research advocates for targeted heat‑wave advisories and preventive measures for older adults. The Stanford team recommends further studies to refine heat tolerance metrics and to develop interventions that mitigate heat‑related morbidity among aging populations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israel opens tenders for West Bank settlement project
content:
Jerusalem – Israeli officials have confirmed plans to develop new housing and infrastructure in the E1 zone, an area east of the city that would link existing settlements to Jerusalem and effectively bisect the occupied West Bank. The proposal, which would create a continuous Israeli presence across the territory, has been met with condemnation from a broad coalition of international actors who argue that it undermines the viability of a two‑state solution.

The United Nations, the European Union and several individual governments have reiterated that the construction would violate international law and exacerbate tensions in the region. Palestinian leaders have warned that the move could trigger widespread unrest, while Israeli authorities contend the development is necessary for security and demographic considerations. Diplomatic discussions continue as the international community seeks to balance settlement activity with efforts to revive negotiations toward a negotiated settlement.
author: BBC World

title: US and South Korea halve Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise after Trump order
content:
The Pentagon and the Republic of Korea’s armed forces confirmed on Wednesday that the two‑nation Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise will be shortened in response to a directive from President Donald Trump. The drill, which began on Monday, is a large‑scale joint training operation that typically runs for a full week.

Under the new schedule, the exercise will now conclude on August 21, six days earlier than the originally planned August 27 finish date. A Defense Department statement said the decision to cut the duration was made to reduce the overall scope of the exercise, in line with the President’s request.

Both sides will adjust their plans accordingly, with the shortened timeline expected to affect the number of maneuvers and the duration of combat simulations conducted during the drill.
author: The Hill

title: Researchers investigate how cat urine scent marks retain identity information over time
content:
**Scent marks remain reliable signals long after the scent is released**  
Researchers have long noted that many mammals, birds, and reptiles use urine and other scent marks to communicate across space and time. These marks persist in the environment even after the animal has left, allowing individuals to assess territory boundaries, reproductive status, and social hierarchy. However, the volatile odor molecules that compose these marks are subject to evaporation, degradation, and chemical transformation, raising the question of how a scent can still convey accurate information about its source.

Recent studies have shown that scent marks are not simple, single‑molecule signals but complex mixtures of compounds with varying chemical stability. Certain hydrocarbons and fatty acids remain intact for days or weeks, while more volatile pheromones provide immediate, short‑term cues. Animals have evolved highly sensitive olfactory receptors tuned to detect these persistent components, enabling them to identify the individual who deposited the mark, its sex, reproductive condition, and even its recent health status. Laboratory experiments tracking the decay of specific urinary compounds confirm that the most informative molecules are those least affected by environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and microbial activity.

These findings underscore the sophistication of chemical communication in the animal kingdom. By relying on a suite of stable and transient molecules, creatures can maintain reliable social and territorial information over extended periods, ensuring effective navigation of complex ecological landscapes.
author: Phys.org

title: Sachin Bansal’s fintech Navi raises first outside capital with $100M Prosus investment
content:
Navi, the fintech startup known for its digital banking platform, has announced a new investment as it moves toward an initial public offering.  While the terms of the deal—including the amount and the identity of the investor—have not been disclosed, the funding is intended to support the company’s expansion plans.

The capital injection comes at a critical juncture for Navi, which is preparing to list on a major stock exchange in the coming months.  The additional resources are expected to help the firm broaden its product suite, enhance its technology infrastructure, and strengthen its balance sheet ahead of the IPO, positioning it for a more robust market debut.

With the investment in place, Navi aims to solidify its competitive standing in the fintech space and provide a stronger foundation for long‑term growth.  The move is seen as a strategic step to ensure the company is well positioned for the heightened scrutiny and capital demands that accompany a public listing.
author: TechCrunch

title: Israel Numbers Palestinian Detainee Foreheads in Qabatiya Raid
content:
Palestinian news outlets reported that a man was found with the number “44” written on his forehead after a raid in the West Bank town of Qabatiya. The incident occurred during a security operation that had been carried out earlier in the day, according to local sources. The man was reportedly injured and was taken to a nearby medical facility for treatment.

The raid, which was conducted by Israeli forces, was part of a broader series of operations in the area aimed at detaining individuals suspected of involvement in recent unrest. While the exact reason for the number on the man’s forehead remains unclear, some observers suggest it could be an identification marker or a symbolic gesture related to the ongoing conflict. The local police have not yet released a statement regarding the man’s identity or the circumstances that led to the marking.

Authorities are investigating the incident, and no further details have been released at this time. The situation remains fluid, and observers are monitoring developments as additional information becomes available.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Jonathan Zimmerman critiques university hiring practices amid Jason Arday controversy
content:
Author Jonathan Zimmerman has recently highlighted the growing tension between merit-based evaluation and identity-focused criteria in higher education. In a piece published in a prominent academic journal, Zimmerman contends that the controversies surrounding former professor Jason Arday and a series of high-profile hiring decisions illustrate a broader shift in university policy away from evidence‑driven assessment toward ideological alignment.

Arday, a scholar in the humanities, was dismissed from his position after a lawsuit alleging discriminatory conduct. The case attracted widespread media coverage and prompted debates about the fairness of the university’s disciplinary procedures. Zimmerman argues that the swift removal of Arday, coupled with similar hiring controversies—such as appointments that emphasize a candidate’s identity background over scholarly credentials—demonstrate a pattern in which institutions prioritize ideological conformity over measurable academic performance. He cites data from recent tenure reviews and hiring panels that show an increasing weight given to diversity statements and political alignment.

Zimmerman’s analysis suggests that this trend may undermine the traditional standards of academic rigor and objectivity. By foregrounding identity politics in hiring and disciplinary processes, universities risk eroding the meritocratic foundations that have historically guided scholarly advancement. The argument underscores a need for clearer, evidence‑based criteria to maintain the integrity of academic evaluation.
author: The Hill

title: Offloading work tasks to AI comes with a cost—to our brains
content:
Government agencies and corporate policy teams are increasingly turning to generative artificial intelligence to accelerate the production of high-stakes policy documents amid compressed deadlines. In recent months, researchers and strategic advisors have reported that AI systems can generate comprehensive draft papers within minutes, delivering organized frameworks, structured arguments, and formatted citations that mirror traditional academic and institutional standards. This rapid output capability is prompting organizations to reassess their research workflows as they balance the demand for swift deliverables with the need for reliable analysis.

The underlying models synthesize information from vast training datasets to produce coherent policy narratives and reference lists
author: Phys.org

title: Study investigates leveraging quantum battery environmental sensitivity for better energy use
content:
Quantum batteries—devices that store energy through quantum mechanical effects—promise faster charging and higher efficiency than conventional batteries. Recent studies suggest that, in principle, these batteries could be charged more quickly by harnessing collective quantum phenomena, potentially transforming portable power and grid storage.

However, researchers have found that the act of connecting a quantum battery to a charger introduces quantum correlations between the two systems. These correlations can lock a portion of the stored energy within the combined battery‑charger complex, preventing it from being extracted as useful work. As a result, the amount of energy that can be delivered to a load is reduced, undermining some of the anticipated performance gains.

The findings highlight a critical challenge for practical quantum energy devices: while quantum effects can enhance storage and charging speeds, they also create entanglement that must be managed to avoid energy loss. Future research will need to develop strategies for decoupling or mitigating these correlations to fully realize the advantages of quantum batteries.
author: Phys.org

title: Australia mushroom killer's lawyers point to jury irregularities at appeal
content: Lawyers for Erin Patterson, the Australian woman convicted of a triple murder involving poisoned food, filed an application on Wednesday to overturn her conviction, alleging that the jury was not properly sequestered during the trial. The 51-year-old was found guilty last year of killing her husband's parents and an elderly aunt by serving them a beef Wellington lunch contaminated with lethal death cap mushrooms in 202
author: France 24

title: Palestinian Authority Lacks Budget for Essential Services
content:
Annette Young announced the arrival of Joost Hiltermann, the International Crisis Group’s Special Adviser for the Middle East and North Africa and a senior training officer.
